course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 2
unit.description: Follow the Spanish, French, Dutch, and British colonies, the regions of British North America, Atlantic trade, slavery, and colonial society from 1607 to 1754.

firstTopic.title: Contextualizing Period 2
firstTopic.summary: The context for European colonization of North America from 1607 to 1754: what had already happened, what each empire wanted, and how environment and rivalry shaped the colonies.

topic.title: Transatlantic Trade
topic.summary: How an Atlantic economy linked Europe, Africa, and the Americas, how Britain tried to control it through mercantilism, and how trade changed American Indian communities.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the Atlantic economy that developed in the 1600s and 1700s?
choices: A single trade route that every ship followed, carrying the same goods from Europe to Africa and then to the Americas
A system in which American Indian nations controlled shipping between Europe and Africa
A trade controlled entirely by the Spanish monarchy and closed to all other empires
A web of trade that moved manufactured goods, colonial products, and enslaved people among three continents
questions.explanation: Goods and people moved among Europe, Africa, and the Americas in many directions, and colonies exported commodities that Europeans valued.
choiceExplanations: Historians use the triangular trade as a model of connected routes, but many voyages did not follow one fixed route.
European merchants and governments controlled Atlantic shipping.
British, French, and Dutch merchants all took part in the Atlantic economy.
Goods and people moved among Europe, Africa, and the Americas in many directions, and colonies exported commodities that Europeans valued.
questions.distinguisher: The single-route choice treats the triangular trade as a fixed route, but it describes a web of connected exchanges.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why European colonies sought new sources of labor?
choices: Colonial economies produced commodities that were valued in Europe, and doing so required large workforces
European governments banned wage labor in their colonies in order to protect their own workers
Native populations had grown so large that colonial officials could not govern them without help
Colonists wanted to reduce their dependence on manufactured goods imported from Europe
questions.explanation: Producing tobacco, sugar, rice, and other exports took many workers, so colonists looked for new sources of labor.
choiceExplanations: Producing tobacco, sugar, rice, and other exports took many workers, so colonists looked for new sources of labor.
Governments did not ban wage labor across their colonies.
Disease and war reduced many Native populations, which added to the demand for labor.
Colonists continued to import manufactured goods from Europe.
questions.distinguisher: Native populations did change, but they shrank rather than grew, which strengthens the demand for workers.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Mercantilism is best described as the belief that
choices: free trade among nations benefits every country equally and requires no government regulation of commerce
a nation grows stronger by exporting more than it imports and by using colonies to supply raw materials
colonies should be allowed to govern their own trade so that they can become prosperous
a nation's power depends mainly on the size of its army and its control of inland territory
questions.explanation: Mercantilists believed national wealth came from a favorable balance of trade and colonies that served the mother country.
choiceExplanations: Mercantilists favored government regulation of trade.
Mercantilists believed national wealth came from a favorable balance of trade and colonies that served the mother country.
Mercantilism treated colonies as sources of raw materials and markets for the mother country.
Mercantilists emphasized wealth from trade, not simply military size.
questions.distinguisher: The near miss mentions national power, but mercantilism located power in trade and wealth.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

choices: colonists pay Parliament a tax on every imported good in order to fund the Royal Navy
colonial merchants trade only with the Netherlands, which had the lowest prices for manufactured goods
colonial trade travel on English or colonial ships and certain goods be sold only within the empire
all manufactured goods made in the colonies be sold in Britain at prices set by Parliament
questions.explanation: The Navigation Acts kept colonial trade within the English empire by regulating the ships and the markets that colonists could use.
choiceExplanations: The Navigation Acts regulated shipping and markets, and they did not impose a tax on every import.
The acts limited trade with the Dutch and other foreign powers.
The Navigation Acts kept colonial trade within the English empire by regulating the ships and the markets that colonists could use.
The acts did not set prices for colonial manufactures.
questions.distinguisher: The tax choice describes a later controversy, whereas the Navigation Acts regulated where goods traveled.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why enforcement of British imperial policies in the colonies was erratic?
choices: Parliament repealed the Navigation Acts soon after passing them because merchants objected
Colonial governors refused every order from the Crown in all of the British colonies
British courts ruled that colonists were exempt from laws that regulated trade
Distance, resistance, and Britain's other concerns made strict enforcement difficult
questions.explanation: The Atlantic was wide, Britain was often busy elsewhere, and colonists and American Indians resisted, so enforcement was uneven.
choiceExplanations: The Navigation Acts remained in force, though enforcement varied.
Governors enforced many orders, but the Atlantic distance and local resistance made enforcement uneven.
Colonists were not legally exempt from the acts.
The Atlantic was wide, Britain was often busy elsewhere, and colonists and American Indians resisted, so enforcement was uneven.
questions.distinguisher: Colonial resistance was real, but it did not mean governors refused all orders or that the acts were repealed.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Trade with Europeans changed American Indian communities mainly by
choices: increasing the flow of goods such as metal tools, cloth, and guns and encouraging dependence on European goods
ending the hunting of furs and deerskins as Native nations moved to European-style farming
requiring Native nations to pay taxes to European monarchs in exchange for protection
giving every Native nation equal access to European goods and weapons through the fur trade
questions.explanation: European goods flowed into Native communities, changing economies, hunting patterns, and the balance among nations.
choiceExplanations: European goods flowed into Native communities, changing economies, hunting patterns, and the balance among nations.
Trade increased the hunting of furs and deerskins.
Trade did not require Native nations to pay taxes to European monarchs.
Access to goods was unequal, which sharpened rivalries among Native nations.
questions.distinguisher: The tax choice describes a colonial relationship, but trade created exchange and dependence without taxation.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a result of the epidemic diseases that spread through contact with Europeans?
choices: Rapid recovery, as Native peoples gained immunity and regained their numbers within a generation
Radical demographic shifts, as some Native communities lost large shares of their populations
A halt to colonization, because European settlers were the main victims of the diseases
The end of the fur trade, because Native hunters refused to meet with European traders
questions.explanation: Diseases such as smallpox killed large shares of communities that had no earlier exposure, reshaping Native societies.
choiceExplanations: Epidemics caused lasting demographic change and populations did not recover so quickly.
Diseases such as smallpox killed large shares of communities that had no earlier exposure, reshaping Native societies.
Native peoples suffered most, and colonization continued.
Trade continued, and it also spread disease.
questions.distinguisher: Immunity develops over time, but the question asks about the immediate and radical effects of epidemics.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a similarity between Britain's economic policies and those of other European empires in the Americas?
choices: Each allowed its colonies to trade freely with the colonies of rival empires
Each placed colonial governments under the control of locally elected assemblies
Each banned the use of enslaved labor in order to protect the wages of workers at home
Each expected its colonies to supply raw materials and buy its manufactured goods
questions.explanation: Mercantilist thinking led European empires to treat colonies as sources of raw materials and markets for finished goods.
choiceExplanations: European empires generally tried to restrict colonial trade to themselves.
Many colonies of other empires were governed by officials sent from Europe.
Britain and other empires used enslaved labor extensively.
Mercantilist thinking led European empires to treat colonies as sources of raw materials and markets for finished goods.
questions.distinguisher: Britain did allow elected assemblies, but that was not a feature shared by all European empires.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Britain strictly enforced the Navigation Acts, which ended smuggling by colonial merchants
Colonial merchants opposed the Navigation Acts because the laws harmed shipbuilders
Britain tried to make the colonies serve its economy, but colonists often resisted or evaded its control
Parliament passed the Navigation Acts to give the colonies control over their own trade
questions.explanation: The passage describes mercantilist laws meant to benefit England, followed by uneven enforcement and resistance.
choiceExplanations: The passage says enforcement was uneven and that many colonists smuggled goods.
The passage says that merchants and shipbuilders gained protected markets.
The passage describes mercantilist laws meant to benefit England, followed by uneven enforcement and resistance.
The acts were designed to benefit England by regulating colonial trade.
questions.distinguisher: The passage mentions that some colonists benefited, so the shipbuilder near miss reverses the evidence.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 2.4, KC-2.2.I.C: the British government tried to incorporate its colonies into an imperial structure to pursue mercantilist aims, but enforcement was erratic
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing how historians describe mercantilism and the Navigation Acts
stimulusBlocks.text:
English leaders in the 1600s believed that a nation grew stronger when it exported more than it imported, and they expected colonies to help by supplying raw materials and buying English manufactured goods. Historians call this approach mercantilism.

To put these ideas into practice, Parliament passed a series of Navigation Acts beginning in 1651 and 1660. The laws required that colonial goods travel on English or colonial ships and that valuable products, such as tobacco and sugar, be shipped only to England or other English colonies. Colonial merchants and shipbuilders gained protected markets, but planters and farmers had fewer places to sell their goods and often paid more for imports.

Britain was far from North America and was often busy with problems at home and in Europe, so enforcement was uneven. Many colonists ignored the rules or smuggled goods, and attempts to tighten control, such as the Dominion of New England in the 1680s, met resistance.

questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a claim and/or argument in a text-based or non-text-based source.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which of the following best explains why colonists were able to evade the Navigation Acts?
choices: Britain was far away and busy with other problems, so enforcement was uneven
Parliament had no authority to pass laws that regulated colonial trade in the 1600s
The acts exempted valuable products such as tobacco and sugar from any regulation
Colonial merchants controlled the ships that were supposed to enforce the laws
questions.explanation: The passage says that distance and Britain's other concerns made enforcement uneven.
choiceExplanations: The passage says that distance and Britain's other concerns made enforcement uneven.
The passage says that Parliament passed the Navigation Acts.
The passage says these goods had to be shipped only to England or other English colonies.
The passage does not say that colonial merchants controlled enforcement.
questions.distinguisher: The tobacco and sugar choice is tempting because those goods mattered, but the passage says they were regulated.

questions.prompt: Which of the following details from the passage best supports the idea that the Navigation Acts affected some colonists differently from others?
choices: Colonial goods had to travel on English or colonial ships under the Navigation Acts of 1651 and 1660
Parliament passed a series of Navigation Acts beginning in 1651 and 1660
The Dominion of New England in the 1680s tried to tighten control over the colonies
Merchants gained protected markets, while planters and farmers had fewer places to sell
questions.explanation: The passage says merchants and shipbuilders benefited, while planters and farmers lost markets and paid more for imports.
choiceExplanations: This describes a rule that applied to all colonial trade.
This gives the dates of the laws and does not show different effects on colonists.
This shows an effort to enforce control and not different effects on groups.
The passage says merchants and shipbuilders benefited, while planters and farmers lost markets and paid more for imports.
questions.distinguisher: The other details are accurate, but they apply to colonists as a whole, so they do not show different effects.
